title: Temporary works failures still follow the same control gaps
excerpt: This week’s HSE and CROSS picture is familiar: platforms used as crash decks with no design, props that ignore the existing structure, and excavations treated as a hole rather than a temporary works item. The lesson is not new kit — it is procedure, competence and load path.
linkedinReady:
Temporary works failures are rarely a mystery. This month’s HSE and CROSS picture repeats the same control gaps: timber platforms used as crash decks with no design or safe load, props designed in isolation from the existing structure, and excavations treated as a hole rather than a temporary works item.

HSE inspector Lucy Ellison-Dunn put it plainly after the Paxton House prosecution: those providing temporary works have a duty to ensure any temporary structure is properly designed and constructed to withstand any foreseeable load.

If your TWC cannot point to a design, a check, a permit and an inspection for the item in use today — it is not controlled.

Read the briefing: https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#TemporaryWorks #BS5975 #ConstructionSafety #TWC

body.p: Industry reporting this month has grouped recent HSE prosecutions around foreseeable construction risks: temporary platforms, excavation access and plant interface. None of these are exotic. They sit in every Temporary Works Register if the register is being used honestly.

Based on published HSE and CROSS material, the same sequence keeps appearing: an item is treated as ‘just temporary’; no design brief is written; loading is assumed rather than calculated; inspection is a tick rather than a competent review; and coordination between principal contractor and specialist contractor is verbal. Standard does not automatically mean low risk — a timber crash deck over a riser shaft is a high-consequence item the moment people work beneath it.

body.h: What a competent TWC should do this week
ul: Walk the live Temporary Works Register against what is actually on site — platforms, crash decks, trench access, makeshift bridges and un-designed packing.
Ask for the design, the check category, the permit-to-load/use and the last competent inspection for every item carrying people or debris.
Treat ‘verbal instruction not to overload’ as a control failure unless a safe load has been calculated and posted.
Escalate incomplete briefs: existing structure capacity, load path to foundation, and who is TWC must be named, not assumed.
